followUpCorrection.observation: A later CI run showed that Node may retain ArrayBuffer backing-store/allocator memory after runtime references are dropped, so immediate post-release process-memory decrease is not a deterministic invariant.
followUpCorrection.repair: Removed the allocator-sensitive release assertion. Release is now tested through explicit release-hook execution, released capability IDs, and absence of runtime bodies from receipts.
followUpCorrection.effectOnMainFinding: None. The eager-vs-Ignition after-materialize ArrayBuffer allocation comparison and exact result equivalence remained the supported evidence.

strongestSupportedClaim: For this deterministic harness, keeping irrelevant capability bodies dormant reduced actual runtime ArrayBuffer working-set allocation while preserving exact result hashes.
boundaries: Does not prove free compute or energy.
Does not prove lower RSS for every runtime or workload.
Does not prove immediate operating-system memory return after release.
Does not prove lower total CPU cost after materialization and scheduling overhead.
Does not prove production-scale savings or universal superiority over eager architecture.
nextGate: Run the same comparison on a realistic modular workload with parsed/indexed state or executable resources and measure peak memory, allocation churn, runtime overhead, reuse, and the break-even point versus eager execution.
